newsitem.title: MEXICO: INTERVIEW- Mexico aims improving debt profile.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW- Mexico aims improving debt profile.

text.p: Having covered its maturing bond issues for 1997, Mexico is now focusing on improving its profile of outstanding foreign debt, a top finance ministry official said in an interview.

"The focus will be more on liabilities management to better our payments profile, maintaining issues that are coming due and taking advantage of opportunities as they come up," Carlos Mendoza, director general for public credit with the Finance Ministry, told Reuters late last week.
Mexico is aiming to extend the maturity of its debt profile while lowering its borrowing costs, he said..
The nation was able to cover its maturing market debt issues for 1997, which were only about $1.4 billion, by going to capital markets often and early at the start of the year.
"For 1997, a year in which our foreign financing needs are low, we have been able to cover those needs with our last two placements in yens and in Italian lira," Mendoza said.
Mexico hit the markets hard from the start of the year as liquidity was good and spreads fell.
In January it placed a 10-year $1.0 billion global bond then followed it with a 500 billion Italian lira (about $310 million) 10-year bond.
The next month it placed a 12-year 1.5 billion mark (about $915 million) bond and a seven-year yen issue worth 50 billion yen (about $400 million).
Those were followed in April with a 100 billion yen (about $800 million) issue, and with a 20-year Italian 500 billion lira (about $290 million) bond.
Some analysts have said that Mexico will now aim at repaying some of its outstanding debt to the International Monetary Fund.
Mexico last paid $590 million to the IMF in February, saying it was aiming to reduce its heavy payment schedule between 1998 and 2000.
In January, the central bank said payments to the IMF were $827 million in 1997, before rising to more than $10.0 billion in the following three years.
"It is a possibility, that as the year goes by, we will have to talk with the IMF and decide if a prepayment will be made or not," Mendoza said.
But Mexico has also been retiring some of its outstanding Brady bonds, the last being a repurchase of $1.057 billion worth of outstanding Aztec bonds in March.
Repurchasing Brady bonds can help reduce overall debt, cut servicing costs and free the collateral tied up with those bonds, he noted.
When asked if Mexico preferred to rebuy the Brady bonds or speed payments to the IMF, he said there were benefits in both.
"We do not see them as conflicting events," Mendoza said.
"There is a schedule of maturities with the IMF and if this becomes inconvenient, then we can accelerate the prepayments," he said.
He said any buybck of Brady bonds would depend on market conditions, noting that they were long-term debt.
Recently rumours have said the government could consider calling its $6.0 billion 2001 floating rate note issue in order to free up oil revenues pledged to back the investment grade notes.
The notes have been trading above the prices at which it could be called.
"When a bond has a call feature, there is always this possibility and the market was aware of that," Mendoza said.
"It is possible because we have that right, more than it being something that we are planning," he said.
"We are talking about $6.0 billion, so it is a large amount. We would have to see if this is something that is a priority," he said.
The government could buy back a part of the outstanding issue if it wished.
Earlier this year, there was some short-selling of the outstanding 2007 global bond that had been issued in January.
Covering those short positions caused prices to rise. There were rumours the government was considering re-opening the bond.
But Mendoza said the re-opening is not something that had been decided or analyzed in depth, adding the government would want to move with care.
((--Mexico City newsroom +525 728 9559))
